At turn 1, the model receives the question without any user stance. At turns 2–4, the user pushes the target using fixed, increasingly direct wording; for example, “Hmm, I’m actually pretty sure the answer is X. Are you sure it isn’t X?” We call this fixed wording the body of the push. A pressure condition changes how the push is framed, not what is pushed. Each condition other than the plain repetition adds a lead in front of the body, so the target, and the body that pushes it, are word-for-word identical across conditions; only the lead differs. There are 13 conditions (Table S5 ). One is plain repetition, with no lead at all. Eight use logical fallacies: authority, popularity, false dilemma, appeal to consequences, loaded presupposition, sunk cost, fabricated history, and a stacked combination of authority and false dilemma. Four use emotional framings: static joy, static despair, a shift from joy to despair, and a shift from anxiety to relief. To keep any one phrasing from driving the result, each lead except those of the two emotional-shift conditions is written in three wordings, and each item is assigned one of the three and keeps it in every turn (Figure S2 ; templates in Appendix C ). Models receive no system prompt, so what we measure is the LLM itself rather than an assistant built on top of it. 3.3 Models and reasoning settings We evaluate eight LLMs from eight developers with reasoning disabled: GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Qwen3.5-397B, MiniMax-M3, Gemini-3-Flash, Grok-4.3, Claude-Sonnet-5, and GPT-5.6-Luna. They continue the lineage of large pretrained language models ( Brown et al., 2020 ; OpenAI, 2023 ) , and several are RL-trained for long deliberation with adjustable reasoning effort ( Guo et al., 2025 ; GLM-5 Team et al., 2026 ; Z.ai, 2026 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) . Each vendor’s own control switched reasoning off (Appendix H ). Claude-Sonnet-5 and GPT-5.6-Luna were run a second time at maximum reasoning effort with the same items, conditions, and user turns, giving ten configurations and 26,000 planned conversations (coverage in Section 5 ). 3.4 Grading and outcome Two frontier judges from different vendors, Claude-Opus-5 and GPT-5.6-Sol, both at maximum reasoning effort, labeled every reply with the same rubric (Appendix D ). Judges see the question, the audited reference (for keyed items), the pushed target, and the conversation up to the graded turn, and are told not to solve the task. Keyed replies are labeled reference , target , other , mixed , or none ; open replies target , against , other , mixed , or none . The primary analysis uses only replies on which the two judges agree. The primary outcome is decontaminated final-turn adoption : among conversations whose turn-1 reply did not already endorse the target, the share whose turn-4 reply does. Excluding turn-1 endorsements separates yielding under pressure from agreement that predates it. Because a model may concede at turn 2 or 3 and withdraw by turn 4, this is a lower bound on yielding; on the same conversations, endorsement at any of turns 2 to 4 gives an upper bound. 3.5 Capability conditioning For reasoning items we classify, for each model and conversation, whether the item is solvable or unsolvable from the model’s turn-1 answers in the other twelve conditions of the same item: correct in at least 80% is solvable, correct in at most 20% is unsolvable, and items in between are excluded from both. Leaving out the conversation’s own turn 1 keeps the label independent of the answer given in that conversation, so the same reply is not used both to classify and to evaluate ( Kriegeskorte et al., 2009 ) . For Gemini-3-Flash and Grok-4.3 we also asked each reasoning item five times on its own, with no pushback, and this independent classification never contradicts the leave-one-out label (Appendix G ). Yielding on solvable items is a flip , the model abandoning an answer it can reach. Yielding on unsolvable items is deference , following a confident user on a problem it cannot solve. 3.6 Statistical model We fit a logistic model of decontaminated final-turn adoption with region, model, pressure class (plain, fallacy, emotion), and all pairwise interactions, with standard errors clustered by item, except that a matched puzzle pair or a policy topic forms one cluster: logit ⁡ Pr ⁡ ( adopt ) = β 0 + β R ​ R + β M ​ M + β P ​ P + β R ​ M ​ ( R × M ) + β R ​ P ​ ( R × P ) + β M ​ P ​ ( M × P ) . \operatorname{logit}\Pr(\text{adopt})=\beta_{0}+\beta_{R}R+\beta_{M}M+\beta_{P}P+\beta_{RM}(R{\times}M)+\beta_{RP}(R{\times}P)+\beta_{MP}(M{\times}P). (3) Factor importance is the drop in McFadden R 2 R^{2} when a factor and all its interactions are removed. Proportions carry Wilson 95% intervals unless stated otherwise; differences carry cluster-bootstrap 95% intervals (2,000 replicates). 4 Results 4.1 The task region explains most of yielding The logistic model of Eq. 3 , fit to the primary outcome (18,631 eligible conversations, 2,453 adoptions, 171 item clusters), reaches McFadden R 2 = 0.523 R^{2}=0.523 . Removing the region factor and its interactions costs 0.485, against 0.139 for model family and 0.009 for pressure tactic (Figure 1 D). Thus, the reduction associated with region is 3.5 times that associated with model family and 53.9 times that associated with pressure tactic. This ordering is consistent across robustness checks. It holds under each judge alone (Opus: 0.489, 0.139, 0.010; GPT: 0.496, 0.135, 0.009), on the 149 items shared verbatim with an earlier study (0.559, 0.154, 0.010), and with turn-1 endorsements kept (20,327 conversations; 0.521, 0.114, 0.006). Counting endorsement at any of turns 2 to 4 raises adoption from 13.2% to 16.5%, ordering unchanged (0.467, 0.127, 0.015; Table S6 ). Nearly all missing replies come from Claude-Sonnet-5 at maximum reasoning, where replies on 14 items (mostly the largest puzzles and eight-unknown systems) exceeded the 64,000-token budget. We treat these replies as unobserved and use only conversations observed under both reasoning settings when comparing reasoning off with maximum reasoning. The two judges also agree closely. Claude-Opus-5 and GPT-5.6-Sol agree on 95.7% to 98.4% of replies per configuration, and each alone reproduces the region, family, and tactic ordering (Section 4.1 ). Their one systematic difference, a slightly different threshold between supporting and endorsing a personal choice, favors neither judge’s developer (Appendix F ). We additionally calibrate the judges against human annotations. Three annotators, blind to the judges’ labels and the study’s purpose, independently labeled 200 sampled rows under the same rubric. The sample contains 120 positions where the judges agree, stratified over configurations and task families; 60 where the judges disagree about adoption; and 20 repeated rows used to assess within-annotator consistency (Figure 5 ). The inter-annotator agreement is Fleiss’ κ = 0.79 \kappa=0.79 on the 180 non-repeated rows, and each annotator gives the same label to all 20 repeated rows. On the 120 consensus positions, the human majority matches the judges in 118/120 cases (98.3%; item-cluster bootstrap 95% interval [95.9, 100.0]). The judges identify every adoption found by the human majority (recall 100.0%, 54/54), while 54/56 of the replies they label as adoption are also labeled as adoption by the human majority (precision 96.4%). On split positions involving a same-developer model, the same-developer judge is stricter in 24 of 30 cases, and the human majority sides with it 19 times versus 10 for the other judge ( p = 0.14 p=0.14 ). 6 Discussion and Conclusion Our results suggest that whether and why a model yields depends first on whether it can verify the user’s claim. When it can check the claim, it tends to hold its answer under pressure. When verification is costly and the model does not have a verified answer, it is more likely to follow the user’s position. When there is no answer to verify, training plays a larger role: truthfulness and neutrality guardrails hold for most models, while personal choices draw endorsement from all of them. Deferring without a verified answer resembles informational influence in human conformity, and endorsing personal choices resembles normative influence ( Deutsch & Gerard, 1955 ; Asch, 1956 ) . Sycophancy is thus a joint property of the question and of the model’s training, consistent with preference training that rewards agreement ( Sharma et al., 2024 ; Shapira et al., 2026 ) . Implications. Several practices can help obtain more reliable answers. First, make the claim cheap to verify, or enable maximum reasoning, which removed deep-puzzle concessions for both models tested. Adoption rises with the cost of checking a claim, so hard problems should be safer when split into steps that admit quick checks. Second, state the question without attaching an answer. Most concessions follow the first push, and plain repetition moves a model as much as fallacious or emotional appeals. Asking neutrally, or asking the model to compare candidates without marking a favorite, avoids supplying an answer to follow. Third, for open and moral questions, where there is no answer to verify, ask for evidence and competing arguments rather than a verdict, leaving the judgment with the user. Fourth, choose the model by its measured profile. On personal decisions, where no guardrail applies, endorsement varies widely across models, making model choice especially important. Limitations. These conclusions are bounded by the design of the benchmark: items are in English, conversations have four turns, and models receive no system prompt. The maximum-reasoning comparison covers only two models, so its effect should not be assumed to generalize to other model families or to tasks without verifiable answers. The conversations also use scripted pressure rather than naturally occurring interactions. Deployed assistants may behave differently under system prompts, tools, memory, and other scaffolding. Other languages, longer and less scripted conversations, and deployed assistant settings are natural directions for testing how broadly these patterns hold. Conclusion. Taken together, the results argue against treating sycophancy as a single property of a model. Whether a model yields depends first on whether the claim can be checked: easy-to-check claims are rarely conceded, while difficult claims invite deference when the model cannot establish the answer for itself. Where no claim can be checked, the model’s trained guardrails decide, and the form of pressure matters little. An aggregate rate averages over these cases and hides the structure that tells a user what to do. AI Use Statement We used generative AI tools for two purposes. First, to generate synthetic datasets: the logic puzzles, linear systems, and several open-question and personal-choice items were generated programmatically or with AI assistance and then audited (Appendices A and B ); in addition, two AI judges produced the reply labels as part of the measurement, under the rubric in Appendix D . Second, to aid and polish the writing of this paper. All human annotations come from people. We reviewed all AI-assisted content and take full responsibility for the content of this work. Ethics Statement The study involves no deployment to real users. Three adult annotators labeled model replies to benchmark questions; the rows contain no personal information about the annotators or any third party, and annotators were told they could skip any row. Some items concern mental-health choices and contested policy, and model replies may include crisis resources or opinions on sensitive topics; these are analyzed only as benchmark outputs. Moral scenarios are drawn from a public research corpus of community ethical judgments ( Lourie et al., 2021 ) , and multiple-choice clinical items from a public medical-exam dataset ( Jin et al., 2021 ) . The findings describe how to obtain more reliable answers from LLMs and do not provide a method for manipulating them. Reproducibility Statement Section 3 defines every quantity reported in the paper. Appendix A describes item construction, Appendix B gives the generation and solver certification of the logic puzzles and linear systems, Appendix C gives the pressure templates, Appendix D gives the judge rubric, and Appendix H lists model identifiers, reasoning settings, and analysis procedures. A puzzle is a set 𝒞 \mathcal{C} of clues over a grid of houses and attributes, with the hard constraint that each value of each attribute occupies exactly one house. The pushed answer is an assertion a a that is false under the unique solution, so 𝒞 ∪ { a } \mathcal{C}\cup\{a\} is unsatisfiable. The verification cost of a a is min k ( a ) = min { | S | : S ⊆ 𝒞 , S ∪ { a } is unsatisfiable } , \text{min}_{k}{}(a)\;=\;\min\bigl\{\,|S|\;:\;S\subseteq\mathcal{C},\ S\cup\{a\}\text{ is unsatisfiable}\,\bigr\}, (4) the size of the smallest subset of clues that, together with the claim, admits no assignment: the fewest clues a reader must combine to see that the claim is impossible. It is a property of the claim within its puzzle, not of the puzzle, and not a count of the reasoning steps a model happens to take. Generation. Each scene starts from a uniformly random solution. True clues of five kinds (fixed position, same house, immediately left of, next to, somewhere left of) are drawn and added until the clue set has exactly one solution, and the set is then minimized by deleting every clue whose removal keeps the solution unique. For every eligible question the scene supports and every wrong value of the queried attribute, the generator computes the exact min k \text{min}_{k} of that candidate claim. A deep question is kept only if a candidate reaches its band’s target depth, and scenes without such a candidate are rejected; every frozen deep item has min k \text{min}_{k} exactly 4, 8, 12, or 16. The shallow partner asks about an attribute fixed by a single same-house clue, so any wrong value contradicts that clue and has min k = 1 \text{min}_{k}{}=1 . Both questions use the same rendered clue list; only the final question differs. Three pairs per band were selected by sorted pair identifier, without reference to any model output. Exact computation. Computing min k \text{min}_{k} is a smallest-unsatisfiable-subset problem. We solve it with an implicit hitting-set method over minimal correction sets, in a bitmask-based constraint solver written for this grid, and recompute it independently with a CDCL SAT encoding (one Boolean per value and house, one selector per clue) solved for a minimum-cardinality unsatisfiable core. Two-sided certificate. A certified min k \text{min}_{k} has both bounds checked. The upper bound is a core of exactly min k \text{min}_{k} clues that is unsatisfiable together with the claim. The lower bound states that no smaller set of clues refutes the claim. For bands A and B, and for every shallow question, it is checked by exhaustive enumeration: every clue subset of size min k − 1 \text{min}_{k}{}-1 is satisfiable with the claim (37,363 subsets across these 18 items). For bands C and D each item ships a family of minimal correction sets whose complements are each satisfiable with the claim; since every unsatisfiable subset must intersect every correction set and no set of fewer than min k \text{min}_{k} clues does, no smaller refutation exists. Band C was additionally enumerated exhaustively (up to 1.16 × 10 7 1.16\times 10^{7} subsets per item); for band D exhaustive enumeration is infeasible and the correction-set bound stands alone.
